label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
To: ashbourne-terrace-chimney
Replying to: p05
Cc: none
Subject: Re: Chimney come down on Ashbourne Terrace in the wind??

I’m a chartered structural engineer with IStructE, but I need to be clear: I’m not acting as an engineer here. This isn’t a commission, I have no PI cover for free advice, and I haven’t been inside any of these houses. This is just me as a neighbour, looking from the pavement opposite at 7 this morning.

Mick, please don’t go into 43 at 9 with props. This really must not go ahead. Propping under a holed roof with a loose stack above is about the worst place you could stand: you’d be underneath the thing you’re trying to hold, the floors may already be carrying debris, and nobody knows the load path now. And please don’t do a loft inspection from inside. That is exactly the sort of close work that needs to wait for the council’s dangerous structures engineer.

What I could see: about 1.2m of no.41’s stack still standing, leaning toward 43; pots gone; mortar washed out at the base. No.43’s front roof slope is holed, and there’s a stepped crack in the brickwork from the bay head up to the first-floor cill, roughly 5–10mm. The bay head looks to have dropped. Loose slates are sitting over the footway at the 43/45 gutter line. The council tape is only across 43’s front garden — not the pavement.

JoJo, your cousin isn’t wrong that Victorian terraces are generally robust. But this is a damaged one, which is a different situation.

Until the council has been, please walk on the other side of the road, especially on the school run. The out-of-hours dangerous structures contact is via the main council number; they know already, but nobody has closed the footway, so keep chasing.

Priya, on Mrs Doherty: it isn’t my decision, and I can’t certify no.45. From the front it looks undamaged, and no.41’s stack sits on the 41/43 party wall, not 45. But I wouldn’t sleep in the front room at 45 tonight; better she goes to family until 45 has been checked.
